sections.h2: How does Maine property tax work?
sections.html:
Maine property tax is set and collected by each municipality, and it is based on what you own on April 1. 36 M.R.S. §502 fixes the status of taxpayers and taxable property as of April 1, and the taxable year runs April 1 to March 31.

Each town sets its own due dates and interest. Under §505 a municipality votes the date or dates taxes are due, the date interest begins (which is also the delinquency date), and the rate. The rate cannot exceed the prime rate plus 3 percentage points as set by the Treasurer of State, and the state posts the maximum by January 20 each year. Towns may allow an early-payment discount of up to 10%.

Because of this, a Maine seller needs to read the town's own bill. Two houses of the same value in neighboring towns can have different due dates, different rates and different ratios.

sections.h2: What does the statewide picture look like?
sections.html:
Maine Revenue Services publishes a yearly Municipal Valuation Return summary. The 2025 report shows a total commitment of $3,650,756,363 on total taxable municipal valuation of $284,892,094,527. In the 2024 report, Cumberland County had the largest valuation at about $70.7 billion, or roughly 28% of the state total, followed by York County at about $53.9 billion. Portland had the largest single municipal valuation at about $14.8 billion.

The certified ratio is the level of assessed value as a percentage of just value, as certified by the assessor under 36 M.R.S. §383 (Property Tax Bulletin 31). A town at 80% assesses at four-fifths of market value, which is one reason you cannot compare bills across towns without comparing the ratio and the rate.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Maine property tax assessment?
sections.html:
You file a written abatement application with the assessors within 185 days of commitment. 36 M.R.S. §841 lets assessors abate for illegality, error or irregularity on an application within that period, or on their own initiative within one year. After one year and up to three years, the municipal officers may act, but they may not abate to correct a valuation error.

Maine Revenue Services Bulletin No. 10 explains the practice:

  • Ask for your property record card and check it for errors such as the wrong build year or acreage.
  • The request must state the amount and the reason, and you carry the burden of proof. Disagreeing with the value is not enough.
  • Useful evidence includes factual mistakes on the card, recent sales of comparable local properties and neighborhood sales data.
  • If the assessor mailed a request for property information under §706-A, answer it, or you may lose the right to appeal.
  • The assessors must decide within 60 days. No written decision in that time means the request is deemed denied.

Taxes are still due on the normal dates while an abatement is pending, according to the Cumberland County assessing page. That page also says the assessment is presumed valid and cites 36 M.R.S. §848-A, under which an assessment is defended if it is accurate within reasonable limits unless a deviation of 10% or more is proven.

sections.h2: Where does an appeal go after the abatement is denied?
sections.html:
After a denial, a taxpayer has 60 days to appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review. Section 843 says that if the board does not issue a written decision within 60 days, the application is deemed denied unless the applicant agrees in writing to a delay.

LevelWhoDeadline or rule

Where no local board exists, Bulletin 10 says the first appeal goes to the county commissioners. Residential property appeals go from the board directly to Superior Court. A taxpayer on property valued at $500,000 or more must pay the greater of the prior year's taxes (up to current taxes) or the undisputed current taxes while the appeal runs, and the appeal is suspended if the taxpayer does not.

sections.h2: What happens if you fall behind on Maine property tax?
sections.html:
Maine uses a tax lien mortgage, not a tax sale. The collector may send a demand notice after 8 months and within one year of commitment, giving 30 days to pay, then records a tax lien certificate at the registry of deeds within 10 days after that period ends (36 M.R.S. §942).

Under §943 the recorded certificate creates a tax lien mortgage that ranks ahead of other liens. If the debt remains unpaid 18 months after recording, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and the right of redemption ends. The treasurer must notify the owner and mortgage holders 30 to 45 days before the foreclosure date.

  • Owners claiming the homestead exemption must receive notice of the hardship abatement process and sources of foreclosure-avoidance help.
  • The taxpayer pays recording and discharge fees plus $13 and any foreclosure notice charge.
  • If the taxpayer dies with a probated will, a probate judge may allow up to 60 more days to redeem.
  • After foreclosure the town holds title and can sell the property.

For an owner in this position, the clock is the 18 months. A sale that closes before then pays the town from proceeds and ends the problem.

sections.h2: Is there hardship relief on a Maine tax bill?
sections.html:
Yes. Under §841(2), municipal officers can abate taxes on a primary residence for a person unable to pay because of hardship or poverty, within three years of commitment. The officers must give a written decision within 30 days of the application, and the proceedings are confidential.

Maine also runs a State Property Tax Deferral Program. You must be 65 or older or unable to work from permanent disability, own a primary residence, have household income under $80,000, and have liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with more than one owner). The state pays the town, then places a lien on the home. Selling the home triggers repayment of the deferred taxes, interest and costs. A new municipal lien prevents future deferral.

The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value by up to $25,000 for a permanent resident, adjusted by the local certified ratio.

sections.h2: How is property tax handled at a Maine closing?
sections.html:
Buyer and seller can agree to split the year's tax on a pro rata basis. 36 M.R.S. §558 says taxes are prorated over the municipality's fiscal year unless the parties agree to a different period.

Remember that the town assesses to whoever owned the property on April 1. If a sale changes the owner, §502 lets the assessor update the records after a declaration of value is filed, and notice of the tax goes to both the new owner and the April 1 owner of record.

The transfer tax is separate. The state charges $2.20 per $500 of value, divided evenly between buyer and seller under §4641-A. Over $1,000,000 an extra $3.80 per $500 applies to the excess.

sections.h2: What should a Maine seller with tax due do first?
sections.html:
1. Call the town tax collector for a payoff figure, including interest and any lien charges.
  2. Check whether a lien certificate has been recorded at the county registry of deeds, and count the months from the recording date.
  3. Ask the assessor for the property record card and compare it against the house.
  4. Note the abatement dates. The 185-day window runs from commitment, which is about when bills first go out.
  5. Tell any buyer about deferral liens, since the state must be repaid at transfer.

If the taxes, a lien and needed repairs all sit on the same house, a cash sale can close without waiting on a buyer's lender, and the tax payoff comes from proceeds. Cash Home Buyers buys Maine houses as-is, and we do not set a price until we have looked at the property.

faqs.q: When is Maine property tax assessed?
faqs.a: As of April 1. Under 36 M.R.S. §502, what you own on April 1 fixes who is taxed for that year, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

faqs.q: How long do I have to apply for a property tax abatement in Maine?
faqs.a: 185 days from the date of commitment. Assessors may also abate on their own within one year, and municipal officers may act on certain errors for up to three years.

faqs.q: Can I appeal an assessor's denial?
faqs.a: Yes. File in writing with the local Board of Assessment Review within 60 days of the decision or deemed denial. Residential cases then go to Superior Court under Rule 80B.
No. Maine uses a tax lien mortgage. If it stays unpaid 18 months after the lien certificate is recorded, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and redemption ends.

faqs.q: Who pays Maine's real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller each pay half, at $2.20 per $500 of value, with an added $3.80 per $500 above $1,000,000.

faqs.q: What happens to a deferred tax balance when I sell?
faqs.a: Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs to the state.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay taxes while an appeal is pending?
faqs.a: Taxes stay due on the normal dates. For property valued at $500,000 or more, you must pay the greater of last year's taxes or the undisputed current taxes.
